items.desc: Choosing an orbit for a satellite always comes with trade-offs. Very low Earth orbit (VLEO), between 100–450 km (62–280 miles), has distinct advantages. items.title: Researchers propose quantum Earth observation for photon-limited environments
items.desc: Have you ever wondered what Earth observation satellites see when they look down at the deep ocean or a dense tropical forest during the dead of night? The answer, for the most part, is nothing. Standard optical sensors require a steady stream of light to function, and in these photon-limited regions, they hit a hard physical boundary. But what if we could rewrite the rules of optical imaging? By borrowing techniques from quantum photonics, we can push beyond these classical limits and unlock a fundamentally new way to observe the darkest and most hidden environments on our planet.

items.title: Room-temperature skyrmion-based synapses could pave the way for energy-efficient AI
items.desc: Artificial intelligence is transforming how information is generated, processed and stored, but its rapid expansion is also driving unprecedented demand for computing power and electricity. items.title: Parakeets, male or female, love a good fight

items.title: Q&A: Is decentralized finance truly independent from traditional markets?
items.desc: With the rise in popularity of the digital assets known as cryptocurrencies over the last decade, the idea of a decentralized financial system that operates outside traditional markets is gaining mainstream appeal. A new analysis from a Penn State researcher, however, suggests that traditional and decentralized markets are more connected than they might seem.

items.title: Anger, hope and compassion do little to spur more climate donations
items.desc: Emotional mechanisms are frequently used to inspire good environmental behavior. But how effective are they at inspiring actual sustainable change? Perhaps not as much as previously believed, according to a new study that challenged participants to put their money where their mouths are.

items.title: Singles in America survey reveals how relationships, marriage, money and family are changing
items.desc: The Kinsey Institute released new data from its annual Singles in America survey, the nation's most comprehensive and longest-running annual study of single adults. Now in its 15th edition, Singles in America has surveyed more than 80,000 people across the United States, creating one of the richest data sets available for understanding shifting relationship patterns, population demographics and social trends.

items.title: Hidden receptor interactions may explain past failures of brain disorder drugs
items.desc: Metabotropic glutamate receptors, which are important but difficult drug targets, interact in surprisingly varied ways with their principal regulatory proteins, according to two new studies led by Weill Cornell Medicine investigators. The findings represent a major step forward in understanding these receptors and how they can be targeted effectively to potentially treat conditions such as epilepsy, depression and anxiety disorders.

items.title: Plague was killing entire families thousands of years before the Black Death
items.desc: Ancient DNA reveals that plague was already killing hunter-gatherers in Siberia 5,500 years ago, long before cities and flea-driven epidemics. The prehistoric strains may have been especially dangerous because they carried a genetic factor capable of provoking severe immune reactions.

items.title: Cancer is rising in younger adults. Faster biological aging may help explain why
items.desc: Cancer rates are rising in adults under 55, and new research suggests accelerated biological aging may be one piece of the puzzle. Scientists found that people from more recent generations tended to have bodies that appeared biologically older than those of earlier generations at the same chronological age. Greater biological age acceleration was linked to a higher risk of early onset cancers, with specific patterns seen for lung, gastrointestinal, uterine and colorectal cancers.

items.title: Chemistry textbooks have been getting this wrong for nearly 100 years
items.desc: A foundational chemistry concept found in textbooks for almost 100 years may have been taught incorrectly. Researchers say the inductive effect in neutral molecules appears to extend only across one chemical bond, rather than gradually weakening over three or four bonds as traditionally taught. The team argues that updating this explanation could make organic chemistry easier to understand and provide a stronger foundation for future research and innovation.

items.title: Hidden brain wiring may help keep the mind sharp as gray matter shrinks
items.desc: Scientists have discovered that the brain’s short-range wiring may help protect cognition even as gray matter shrinks with age. Healthier connections just beneath the brain’s surface were linked to better language skills and appeared to weaken the impact of gray matter loss.

items.title: This German submarine sank in 1917. It’s still leaking TNT
items.desc: A World War I submarine wreck off Denmark is leaking TNT into the surrounding water, seabed, and marine life more than a century after it sank. Scientists warn that thousands of similar wrecks could pose growing environmental risks as they continue to corrode.

items.title: Crocodiles are famous for finding their way home. These ones didn’t
items.desc: Captive-raised saltwater crocodiles released into Bangladesh’s Sundarbans surprised scientists by settling into the wild rather than trying to return to their breeding facility. The result suggests that releasing larger, mature captive crocodiles could help restore depleted populations more successfully than relying only on vulnerable hatchlings.

items.title: AI uncovers hidden Ozempic side effects across 400,000 Reddit posts
items.desc: AI analysis of 400,000 Reddit posts found that users of drugs such as Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, and Zepbound reported unexpected symptoms including menstrual changes, chills, hot flashes, and fatigue. Researchers cannot say the medications caused these problems, but the patterns may reveal overlooked signals worth studying.

items.title: One Mount Etna eruption took weeks. Another happened in hours
items.desc: Mount Etna’s ancient eruptions followed radically different paths, with some magma lingering near the surface for weeks while other magma raced upward from nearly 30 kilometers deep in just hours. Scientists traced the difference to volcanic gases such as carbon dioxide and water, offering a powerful new way to understand and potentially anticipate explosive eruptions.

items.title: Scientists find a new layer of Alzheimer’s hidden in the genome
items.desc: Scientists found that the 3D organization of DNA is disrupted in several types of brain cells affected by Alzheimer’s disease, altering how important genes are switched on and off. The discovery reveals a previously underexplored layer of the disease that could open new paths for understanding and eventually treating Alzheimer’s.

items.title: Physicists can’t agree on how the Universe works
items.desc: A massive worldwide survey of physicists has revealed surprisingly little agreement about some of the universe’s biggest mysteries. No majority backed the standard cosmological model, a leading explanation for dark matter, or any single theory of quantum gravity. One area of stronger agreement stood out: 68% said the Big Bang does not necessarily represent the beginning of time. Researchers say the divisions show just how alive and unsettled the frontiers of physics remain.

items.title: NASA-backed scientists turn plastic waste into edible cookies
items.desc: Scientists have engineered yeast to turn PET plastic and agricultural waste into ingredients for protein-rich, 3D-printed cookies called µBites. Developed partly for NASA’s Deep Space Food Challenge, the system can produce proteins, fats, vitamins, and even vanilla flavoring from waste materials. Researchers hope the unusual technology could eventually help address both plastic pollution and food insecurity, while also supplying food in extreme environments such as deep-space missions.

items.title: Global warming is breaking a 400-year climate link between two oceans
items.desc: The Indian and Pacific oceans have been climatically linked for centuries, but scientists say that connection is now breaking down in an exceptional way. Ancient climate records suggest volcanoes disrupted the relationship in the past, while today human-caused warming appears to be driving a much more unusual shift.

items.title: Physicists discover a hidden “curveball” in quantum light
items.desc: Researchers have experimentally demonstrated the optical Magnus effect for the first time, revealing that a tightly focused laser interacts most strongly with an atom slightly away from the beam’s center. The unexpected shift is similar to the physics that makes a spinning table tennis ball curve through the air. Because lasers are used to control qubits, the effect could create errors in quantum computers, but it might also provide a new way to couple qubits together.

items.title: Venus’s pale yellow clouds may hide something surprisingly dark
items.desc: A century-old mystery in Venus’s clouds just became more intriguing, as scientists calculated how strongly the unidentified material behind its dark ultraviolet patterns must absorb light. The results sharply narrow the possibilities and could help future spacecraft determine whether the mysterious substance is organic, inorganic, or something unexpected.

items.title: Scientists discover a hidden switch that shuts down inflammation
items.desc: Scientists have uncovered a natural braking system that helps the immune system switch off inflammation and prevent harmful immune cells from building up. Boosting this pathway in people reduced inflammation-related immune changes and sped up pain relief, pointing toward potential new treatments for chronic inflammatory diseases.

items.title: The People Not Worth Replacing
items.desc: At first glance, MAGA’s fear of immigrants and the rest of America’s fear of data centers have many similarities, with each reflecting insecurities about one’s place in a changing economy. But while the first fear tells natives that their place is valuable, the second assumes that it will soon be worth nothing.

items.title: What Amodei’s Call for an AI Pause Gets Wrong
items.desc: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s recent appeal for a pause on AI development is a welcome one. But while AI companies do indeed need more breathing space to consider the full impact of their inventions before releasing them to the market, self-interested oversight is not the kind of governance we need.

items.title: The Strategic Asset Europe Has Overlooked
items.desc: Europe’s soil is gradually dying, and yet the continent has still not recognized it as a strategic asset. Fortunately, the EU has many of the tools it needs to act, but doing so will require an overarching framework that helps farmers access financial rewards for measurable soil outcomes.

items.title: Who Is Responsible for Nepal’s Tragedy?
items.desc: The devastating floods in Nepal demonstrate what happens when reckless development puts climate-vulnerable communities in harm’s way. They also highlight a climate-finance system that is unable to provide the funds countries need in the immediate aftermath of such disasters.

items.title: Europe Must Choose Between Power and Dependence
items.desc: European citizens do not want “more Europe” in the abstract, but rather a European Union that is capable of protecting, investing, anticipating, deciding, and acting whenever national-level policymaking is insufficient. In today’s world, ensuring citizens’ control over their future requires the freedom to act together.

items.title: Progressive Economics Is Delivering
items.desc: By combining fiscal responsibility, growth, and social development, progressive governments in Brazil and Spain have improved millions of people’s lives and refuted the hoary belief that conservatives are better stewards of the economy. Such a successful alternative model could not have come at a better time.

items.title: The Agentic Information Economy
items.desc: An internet populated and run by AI agents will need not just reliable data but also a broader information ecology capable of questioning its own inputs and transmitting corrections where they are needed if information changes. But whether this will serve private interests or the public good remains to be seen.

items.title: Who Owns What AI Learns?
items.desc: Since frontier AI models have already consumed much of the readily available stock of public knowledge on the internet, what remains is the valuable tacit knowledge embedded within organizations. Whoever sets the terms of how this knowledge is teased out and transferred will set the terms of the next economy.

items.title: America First Is Jeopardizing Taiwan’s Greatest Asset
items.desc: Rather than strengthening Taiwan, US demands for market access, technology investment, and defense capabilities are deepening political polarization and eroding the island’s ability to build consensus just when it needs it most. The timing could hardly be worse.

items.title: Technology Is Not Above the Law
items.desc: In arguing for a regulatory regime that is skewed entirely toward freeing developers to build online services, rather than placing any social obligations on them, the AI industry is using a playbook that Silicon Valley wrote 30 years ago. This time, however, the public seems less inclined to buy the industry's argument.

items.title: China’s Platform State and the AI Race
items.desc: Balancing regulation with innovation is never easy, and the Chinese government’s robust support for AI could lead to inefficiency and excess. But the “platform state” model, combined with other strengths, has enabled China to achieve dominance in multiple strategic sectors, while enhancing its resilience.

items.title: Which Future for Online Life?
items.desc: By articulating a vision of the future that seems inevitable, technology industry leaders want to create the impression that the surrender of privacy and other defining trends of the current moment cannot be stopped. But predictions become self-fulfilling prophecies only if we believe them and act accordingly.

items.title: When Words Are No Longer for Us
items.desc: Owing to the proliferation of large language models throughout our software and social systems, we are now undergoing a textpocalypse, marked by not just a deluge of slop but a fundamental unmooring of language and text from lived human experience. The first victim is likely to be the internet itself.

items.desc: The original vision of the internet as a democratizing force failed to account for the manner in which power would concentrate, attention would be monetized, and public discourse would be manipulated. In Europe and elsewhere, these lessons now must inform how we govern generative AI.
